source_text: Ματαιότατοι δὲ πάντων καὶ οἱ περὶ τὰς τέχνας πονούμενοι· ἀλλ' εὐθηνήσει μὲν ὁ γεωργὸς, μήτε σπέρματα καταβάλλων, μήτε δρεπάνην θηξάμενος· ὑπερπλουτήσει δὲ ὁ ἔμπορος, κἂν βούληται, κἂν μὴ, τῆς εἱμαρμένης αὐτῷ συναθροιζούσης τὰ χρήματα. Αἱ δὲ μεγάλαι τῶν Χριστιανῶν ἐλπίδες φροῦδαι ἡμῖν οἰχήσονται, οὔτε δικαιοσύνης τιμωμένης, οὔτε κατακρινομένης τῆς ἁμαρτίας, διὰ τὸ μηδὲν κατὰ προαίρεσιν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιτελεῖσθαι. Ὅπου γὰρ ἀνάγκη καὶ εἱμαρμένη κρατεῖ, οὐδεμίαν ἔχει χώραν τὸ πρὸς ἀξίαν, ὃ τῆς δικαιοκρισίας ἐξαίρετόν ἐστι. Καὶ πρὸς μὲν ἐκείνους, ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον. Οὔτε γὰρ ὑμεῖς πλειόνων δεῖσθε λόγων παρ' ἑαυτῶν ὑγιαίνοντες, ὅ τε καιρὸς οὐκ ἐνδίδωσι πέρα τοῦ μέτρου πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἀποτείνεσθαι. 6.8 Πρὸς δὲ τὰ ἑξῆς τῶν ῥημάτων ἐπανέλθωμεν. Ἔστωσαν, φησὶν, εἰς σημεῖα, καὶ εἰς καιροὺς, καὶ εἰς ἡμέρας, καὶ εἰς ἐνιαυτούς. Εἴρηται ἡμῖν τὰ περὶ τῶν σημείων. Καιροὺς δὲ ἡγούμεθα λέγειν τὰς τῶν ὡρῶν ἐναλλαγάς· χειμῶνος, καὶ ἔαρος, καὶ θέρους, καὶ μετοπώρου· ἃς εὐτάκτως περιοδεύειν ἡμᾶς τὸ τεταγμένον τῆς κινήσεως τῶν φωστήρων παρέχει. Χειμὼν μὲν γὰρ γίνεται, τοῖς νοτίοις μέρεσι τοῦ ἡλίου προσδιατρίβοντος, καὶ πολὺ τὸ νυκτερινὸν σκίασμα περὶ τὸν καθ' ἡμᾶς τόπον ἀποτελοῦντος· ὥστε καταψύχεσθαι μὲν τὸν περὶ γῆν ἀέρα, πάσας δὲ τὰς ὑγρὰς ἀναθυμιάσεις συνισταμένας περὶ ἡμᾶς, ὄμβρων τε αἰτίαν καὶ κρυμῶν καὶ νιφάδος ἀμυθήτου παρέχειν. Ἐπειδὰν δὲ ἐπανιὼν πάλιν ἀπὸ τῶν μεσημβρινῶν χωρίων ἐπὶ τοῦ μέσου γένηται, ὥστε ἐξίσου μερίζειν νυκτὶ πρὸς ἡμέραν τὸν χρόνον, ὅσῳ πλεῖον τοῖς ὑπὲρ γῆς προσδιατρίβει τόποις, τοσούτῳ κατὰ μέρος ἐπανάγει τὴν εὐκρασίαν. Καὶ γίνεται ἔαρ, πᾶσι μὲν φυτοῖς τῆς βλαστήσεως ἀρχηγὸν, δένδρων δὲ τοῖς πλείστοις παρέχον τὴν ἀναβίωσιν, ζῴοις δὲ χερσαίοις καὶ ἐνύδροις ἅπασι τὸ γένος φυλάσσον ἐκ τῆς τῶν ἐπιγινομένων διαδοχῆς. Ἐκεῖθεν δὲ ἤδη πρὸς θερινὰς τροπὰς ἐπ' αὐτὴν τὴν ἄρκτον ἀπελαύνων ὁ ἥλιος, τὰς μεγίστας ἡμῖν τῶν ἡμερῶν περιίστησι. Καὶ διὰ τὸ ἐπὶ πλεῖστον προσομιλεῖν τῷ ἀέρι, αὐτόν τε καταφρύσσει τὸν ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς ἡμῶν ἀέρα, καὶ τὴν γῆν πᾶσαν καταξηραίνει, τοῖς τε σπέρμασιν ἐκ τούτου συνεργῶν πρὸς τὴν ἅδρησιν, καὶ τοὺς τῶν δένδρων καρποὺς κατεπείγων ἐπὶ τὴν πέψιν· ὅτε καὶ φλογωδέστατός ἐστιν ἑαυτοῦ ὁ ἥλιος, βραχείας ποιῶν τὰς σκιὰς ἐπὶ τῆς μεσημβρίας, διὰ τὸ ἀφ' ὑψηλοῦ τὸν περὶ ἡμᾶς καταλάμπειν τόπον. Μέγισται γάρ εἰσιν ἡμερῶν, ἐν αἷς βραχύταταί εἰσιν αἱ σκιαὶ, καὶ βραχύταται πάλιν ἡμέραι, αἱ τὰς σκιὰς ἔχουσαι μακροτάτας. Καὶ τοῦτο παρ' ἡμῖν τοῖς ἑτεροσκίοις λεγομένοις ὅσοι τὰ ἀρκτῷα τῆς γῆς ἐποικοῦμεν· ἐπεὶ εἰσί γε ἤδη τινὲς οἱ κατὰ δύο ἡμέρας τοῦ παντὸς ἐνιαυτοῦ καὶ ἄσκιοι παντελῶς κατὰ τὴν μεσημβρίαν γινόμενοι, οὓς κατὰ κορυφῆς ἐπιλάμπων ὁ ἥλιος, ἐξίσου πανταχόθεν περιφωτίζει, ὥστε καὶ τῶν ἐν βάθει φρεάτων τὸ ὕδωρ διὰ στομίων στενῶν καταλάμπεσθαι· ὅθεν αὐτούς τινες καὶ ἀσκίους καλοῦσιν. Οἱ δὲ ἐπέκεινα τῆς ἀρωματοφόρου ἐπ' ἀμφότερα τὰς σκιὰς παραλλάσσουσιν. Μόνοι γὰρ ἐν τῇ καθ' ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένῃ ἐπὶ τὰ νότια κατὰ τὴν μεσημβρίαν τὰς σκιὰς ἀποπέμπουσιν· ὅθεν αὐτούς τινες καὶ ἀμφισκίους ὠνόμασαν.
thought_title: The seasons follow the ordered motion of the lights
orientation: Basil is expounding Genesis 1:14, explaining that the lights serve 'for seasons' by governing the orderly cycle of winter, spring, summer, and autumn.
pass_a_gloss: But most vain of all are also those who toil over the arts; but the farmer will prosper, neither casting seeds nor sharpening a sickle; and the merchant will become exceedingly rich, whether he wishes or not, since fate gathers the wealth for him. And the great hopes of the Christians will depart from us as empty, neither righteousness being honored nor sin being condemned, because nothing is accomplished by human beings according to choice. For where necessity and fate rule, the principle of desert has no place, which is the special feature of just judgment. And against those men, so much for that. For neither do you need more words, being sound in yourselves, nor does the occasion allow us to extend beyond measure against them. 6.8 But let us return to the next words. Let them be, he says, for signs and for seasons and for days and for years. The matters concerning the signs have been spoken by us. And we understand seasons to mean the alternations of the hours: of winter and spring and summer and autumn; which the ordered motion of the lights provides for us to pass through in good order. For winter occurs when the sun lingers in the southern regions and produces much nocturnal shadow around our region; so that the air around the earth is cooled, and all the moist exhalations gathered around us provide the cause of rains and frosts and immense snow. But whenever the sun, returning again from the southern regions, comes to the middle, so as to divide the time equally between night and day, by as much as it lingers more over the places above the earth, by so much it gradually brings back the mild temperature. And spring occurs, the beginning of sprouting for all plants, and providing for most trees their revival, and for all land and water animals preserving their kind through the succession of offspring. From there already the sun, driving toward the summer solstice at the very Bear, brings about for us the longest of days. And because it consorts with the air for the longest time, it both scorches the air above our heads and dries out all the earth, and thereby cooperates with the seeds toward their ripening, and urges the fruits of the trees toward maturity; at which time the sun is most fiery of itself, making the shadows short at midday, because it illuminates the region around us from on high. For the days are longest in which the shadows are shortest, and again the days are shortest which have the longest shadows. And this is the case among us who are called 'different-shadowed,' as many of us as inhabit the northern parts of the earth; since there are already some who during two days of the whole year become completely shadowless at midday, whom the sun, shining down from overhead, illuminates equally from every side, so that even the water in deep wells is illuminated through narrow openings; whence some also call them 'shadowless.' But those beyond the spice-bearing land cast their shadows alternately to both sides. For alone in our inhabited world they send their shadows toward the south at midday; whence some have also named them 'double-shadowed.'

lemmas.gloss: casting shadow to one side only

choices.why: Basil uses this term for the deterministic force he is refuting; 'fate' captures the impersonal necessity he opposes to human choice.
The glossary requires 'lights' for the heavenly bodies created on the fourth day.
Basil is explaining a technical geographical term; the literal rendering preserves the etymological sense he is unpacking.
Basil explicitly glosses the term as those who cast no shadow at midday; the literal English matches his explanation.
Basil explains the term as casting shadows alternately to both sides; the literal rendering preserves his etymological point.
This is Basil's key term for free moral agency, contrasted with fate; 'choice' is the standard philosophical rendering.

pass_b_english: But the most foolish of all are those who labor at the crafts. The farmer will prosper, they say, without sowing seed or sharpening a sickle, and the merchant will become exceedingly rich whether he wants to or not, because fate gathers wealth for him. Our great Christian hopes will vanish into nothing, since righteousness is not honored and sin is not condemned, because nothing is accomplished by human choice. For where necessity and fate rule, there is no place for what is deserved, which is the special mark of just judgment. So much for those people. You do not need more words from me, since you are sound in your own thinking, and the time does not allow me to stretch out my response to them beyond measure.

Let us return to the next words of the text. "Let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years," it says (Genesis 1:14). We have already spoken about the signs. By seasons, I think he means the alternations of the year's periods: winter, spring, summer, and autumn. The ordered movement of the lights causes us to pass through these in good order. Winter comes when the sun lingers in the southern regions and produces a long stretch of nighttime shadow over our part of the earth, so that the air around the earth grows cold, and all the moist vapors gather around us and bring about rain, frost, and boundless snow. But when the sun returns again from the southern regions and reaches the midpoint, so that it divides the time equally between night and day, the more it lingers over the places above the earth, the more it gradually brings back a mild temperature. Then spring comes, which is the beginning of sprouting for all plants, grants renewal of life to most trees, and preserves the race of all land and water creatures through the succession of their offspring. From there the sun drives on toward the summer solstice, toward the Bear itself, and brings about the longest days for us. Because it stays in contact with the air for the greatest length of time, it scorches the air above our heads and dries out the whole earth, and in this way it helps the seeds to mature and urges the fruits of the trees toward ripeness. At that time the sun is at its most blazing, making the shadows short at midday, because it shines down on our region from on high. The longest days are those in which the shadows are shortest, and the shortest days are those in which the shadows are longest. This is true for us who are called different-shadowed, all of us who inhabit the northern parts of the earth. For there are already some people who, for two days of the whole year, become completely shadowless at midday. The sun shines down on them from directly overhead and illuminates them equally from every side, so that even the water in deep wells is lit up through their narrow openings. That is why some call them shadowless. But those beyond the spice-bearing land cast their shadows alternately to both sides. They are the only ones in our inhabited world who send their shadows toward the south at midday. That is why some have named them double-shadowed.

last_rejected.quote: The farmer will prosper, they say, without sowing seed or sharpening a sickle
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀλλ' εὐθηνήσει μὲν ὁ γεωργός, μήτε σπέρματα καταβάλλων, μήτε δρεπάνην θηξάμενος
last_rejected.why: Missing 'they say' makes Basil state absurdity as his own view, not opponents'.
last_rejected.fix: The farmer will prosper, they say, without sowing seed or sharpening a sickle
last_rejected.ruling: No 'they say' in source; ἀλλ' εὐθηνήσει introduces opponents' claim implicitly via context.

last_rejected.why: 'Different-shadowed' is opaque; 'heteroski' or 'those with changing shadows' needed.
last_rejected.ruling: ἑτεροσκίοις means 'different-shadowed'; literal rendering is within normal range, not a mistranslation.

last_rejected.why: 'Double-shadowed' suggests two shadows; ἀμφισκίοις means shadows falling both ways/north and south.
last_rejected.fix: amphiski (those whose shadows fall both ways)
last_rejected.ruling: ἀμφισκίους means shadows on both sides; 'double-shadowed' captures this within normal semantic range.
